8
AP Calculus AB and BC 
return to Contents

Technology Needs and Use of Graphing 
Calculators

Technology should be used throughout the course as a tool to explore concepts. 
Specifically, the use of a graphing calculator is considered an integral part of 
the AP Calculus courses, and it is required on some portions of the AP Exam. 
Professional mathematics organizations such as the National Council of Teachers 
of Mathematics (NCTM), the Mathematical Association of America (MAA), and 
the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) Board on Mathematical Sciences and 
Their Applications have strongly endorsed the use of calculators in mathematics 
instruction and testing.

A graphing calculator appropriate for use on the AP Exam is expected to have 
the built-in capabilities to plot the graph of a function within an arbitrary viewing 
window, find the zeros of functions (solve equations numerically), numerically 
calculate the derivative of a function, and numerically calculate the value of a 
definite integral. For free-response questions, when results are obtained using 
one of these required calculator capabilities, students are required to write 
the setup (e.g., the equation being solved, or the derivative or definite integral 
being evaluated) that leads to the solution, along with the result produced by 
the calculator. Use of other built-in calculator features or programs require the 
mathematical steps necessary to produce the results.

Graphing calculators are valuable tools for exploring multiple components of 
the mathematical practices, including using technology to develop conjectures, 
connecting concepts to their visual representations, solving problems, and 
critically interpreting and accurately reporting information. The AP Calculus 
courses also support the use of other technologies that are available to students 
and encourage teachers to incorporate technology into instruction in a variety of 
ways as a means of facilitating discovery and reflection.

Appropriate examples of graphing calculator use in AP Calculus include, but are 
certainly not limited to, the following:

	Bullet Zooming to reveal local linearity

Bullet Constructing a table of values to conjecture a limit

	Bullet Developing a visual representation of Riemann sums approaching a definite 

integral

	Bullet Graphing Taylor polynomials to understand intervals of convergence for Taylor 

series

	Bullet Drawing a slope field and investigating how the choice of initial condition 

affects the solution to a differential equation
